questions.q: Per this lesson, what defines 'sensitive data'?
options: Any data stored in an encrypted database
Data that, if exposed, causes harm to the specific person it describes
Any data a company has not yet made public
Data older than a defined retention period
questions.explain: Sensitive data (health records, biometrics, orientation, religion, financial account numbers) is defined by personal harm to the individual it's about if it's exposed — embarrassment, discrimination, or fraud.

questions.q: Which of these is the best example of confidential data that is NOT personally sensitive?
options: A customer's health diagnosis
An employee's biometric fingerprint template
A company's unreleased merger and acquisition plan
A person's religious affiliation
questions.explain: An unreleased M&A plan is protected for business reasons (competitive advantage, insider-trading exposure) with no individual personally harmed if it leaks — the defining trait of confidential-but-not-sensitive data.

questions.q: Why does a leaked health record primarily concern the individual rather than the company storing it, per this lesson?
options: Because companies are legally barred from holding health records
Because the harm — embarrassment, discrimination, potential fraud — falls mainly on the person the record is about, not on the company's trade secrets
Because health records are never considered valuable business data
Because health records are classified the same way as source code
questions.explain: The lesson distinguishes sensitive data precisely because the real-world harm lands on the individual the data describes, unlike confidential data where the business itself bears the risk.

questions.q: Which example does the lesson give of data that is genuinely BOTH sensitive and confidential at once?
options: A public company's quarterly earnings press release
An executive's salary and health benefits file
A publicly posted job listing
A company's published privacy policy
questions.explain: An executive's compensation and health file is sensitive to that individual (personal harm if exposed) and confidential to the company (it doesn't want compensation structures made public) — both categories apply simultaneously.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say this sensitive/confidential distinction matters for Chapter 2's classification labels?
options: Because classification schemes only need to consider business risk, never personal harm
Because a labeling scheme has to account for both personal-harm risk and business risk, or it will under-protect one category while focusing only on the other
Because sensitive and confidential data always receive the exact same classification label
Because classification only applies to data that is neither sensitive nor confidential
questions.explain: A classification scheme built only around business confidentiality would under-protect personal health data, and one built only around personal sensitivity would under-protect unreleased financials — the labels in Chapter 2 have to cover both risks.
